body:
### Problem

`GET /api/messages/{address}` returns the entire mailbox on every call. With no cursor, clients download everything again on each poll and deduplicate locally.

### Agreed design (Discord, with the mentors)

- **Message ID** = hash of `to | from | payload`, so the same payload sent to two recipients gets two different IDs. A retried identical send becomes a no-op instead of a duplicate.
- **Per-mailbox sequence number** on every message (1, 2, 3, … per recipient). Per mailbox rather than global, so a client can't infer how much traffic other mailboxes get.
- `GET /api/messages/{address}?after=<seq>&limit=<n>` returns only messages with a higher seq. The client keeps track of the last seq it handled. The server keeps no per-client state, so each device has its own cursor.

### Implementation notes

- Sequence numbers must never be reused. With `MAX(seq)+1`, a deleted or purged message's number would be handed out again, and a client already past that number would never see the new message. So the counter has to live in its own table.
- Two concurrent sends to the same mailbox must not read the same counter value.
- Existing databases need a migration that numbers the messages already stored in arrival order.
- Without `after`/`limit`, the endpoint must keep returning the whole mailbox, so existing clients are unaffected.
title: Add per-mailbox sequence numbers and content-derived message IDs

body:
### Problem

`extractIP` in `internal/middleware/ratelimit.go` keys the rate limiter on the **leftmost** `X-Forwarded-For` entry, falling back to `X-Real-IP`. The client controls both, so sending a different value on every request gets it a fresh bucket each time.

Reproduced locally with `rate_limit: 30`:

| Requests | Header | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 35 | fixed `X-Forwarded-For: 9.9.9.9` | 30 × 200, then 5 × 429 |
| 35 | rotating `X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.$i` | 35 × 200 — limiter never engages |

This matters most for hosted deployments, which always sit behind a proxy.

### Proposed fix

Add `security.trusted_proxies: N` (env `RELAY_SECURITY_TRUSTED_PROXIES`):

- `0` (default): ignore forwarding headers and use `RemoteAddr`, so the safe behaviour is the default.
- `N`: take the Nth `X-Forwarded-For` entry **from the right**, the last one a trusted proxy appended. Entries further left are never read.

Stop reading `X-Real-IP`. Document the setting for Nginx, Cloudflare Tunnel and hosting platforms, because deployments behind a proxy will need to set it.

Discussed with the mentors on Discord (Issue 2 in the security thread).
title: Rate limiter can be bypassed by spoofing X-Forwarded-For

body:
## Problem

The relay serves no CORS headers at all — confirmed via \`grep -rn "cors\|CORS\|Access-Control"\` across the Go source, which returns nothing, and there's no middleware registered for it in \`cmd/relay/main.go\`'s handler chain (\`API Key → Rate Limiter → Router\`).

Any browser-based consumer that calls the relay directly (i.e. without routing through a same-origin reverse proxy) hits a blocked preflight:

\`\`\`
Access to fetch at 'https://thrubox-server.onrender.com/api/messages' from origin 'https://<consumer-app>'
has been blocked by CORS policy: Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check:
No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.
\`\`\`

This was already anticipated in the ThruBox-Client consumer docs/comments (see Chainvoice's \`relayClient.js\` and \`vite.config.js\`), which document proxying as the only supported workaround today:

> "The relay serves no CORS headers, so a direct cross-origin request from the browser fails its preflight... Production is expected to reach the relay through a reverse proxy that supplies CORS."

That workaround is fine for consumers willing to run their own reverse proxy, but ThruBox-Server is published as a general-purpose relay (npm SDK + GHCR image) — any consumer that wants to call it directly from the browser without standing up a proxy currently can't.

## Proposed fix

Add CORS middleware to the handler chain in \`cmd/relay/main.go\`, alongside the existing \`APIKeyAuth\`/\`RateLimiter\` middleware:

- Handle preflight \`OPTIONS\` requests explicitly (the current \`http.ServeMux\` routes have no \`OPTIONS\` handler, so preflights currently 404 in addition to missing headers).
- Set \`Access-Control-Allow-Origin\`, \`Access-Control-Allow-Methods\` (GET, POST, DELETE), and \`Access-Control-Allow-Headers\` (at minimum \`Content-Type\`, and \`X-API-Key\` when \`security.api_key\` is configured).
- Make allowed origins configurable (new \`security.allowed_origins\` config key + \`RELAY_SECURITY_ALLOWED_ORIGINS\` env override, following the existing pattern in \`internal/config/config.go\`) rather than hardcoding \`*\`, so self-hosted operators can restrict it if they want to.
- Document the new config in README's Configuration table, and note that consumers can now either proxy (existing approach) or call the relay directly if their origin is allowlisted.

## Notes

- Not urgent for Chainvoice's current deployment specifically — that's being fixed independently via a Vercel rewrite (same-origin proxy), matching the already-documented intended setup.
- This is about unblocking *other* ThruBox consumers who don't have a proxy in front of the relay.
title: Add CORS support for direct cross-origin browser clients

body:
### Problem

`main.go` loads configuration with a relative path:

```go
cfg, err := config.Load("config.yaml")
```

The runtime stage of the Dockerfile sets no `WORKDIR`, so the process runs from
`/` and looks for `/config.yaml`. The Dockerfile copies the file to
`/etc/relay/config.yaml` instead:

```dockerfile
COPY --from=builder /app/config.yaml /etc/relay/config.yaml
```

`config.Load` treats a missing file as "use defaults", so this fails silently.
Containerised deployments run on hardcoded defaults, and any change a user makes
to `config.yaml` is ignored with no warning. It is invisible today only because
the defaults happen to match the shipped config.

### Fix

Make the config path configurable, e.g. a `RELAY_CONFIG_PATH` environment
variable defaulting to `config.yaml`, and set it to `/etc/relay/config.yaml` in
the Dockerfile. Setting `WORKDIR /etc/relay` would also work.

Consider logging at startup which config file was loaded, or that none was found
and defaults are in use — the silence is what makes this hard to notice.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A modified `config.yaml` baked into the image takes effect
- [ ] Env var overrides still win over the file
- [ ] Startup log states which config path was used, or that defaults are in use
- [ ] No config file present → still starts on defaults (unchanged behaviour)
title: config.yaml is never read inside the Docker image

body:
### Problem

The server only reads `RELAY_SERVER_PORT` (`internal/config/config.go`, `applyEnvOverrides`). Most managed platforms — Render, Railway, Heroku, Cloud Run inject a `PORT` variable instead and expect the process to bind to it. Right now ThruBox ignores it and binds to 3000, so deploys either fail health checks or depend on the platform's port auto-detection.

Supporting `PORT` makes ThruBox deployable on those platforms with no extra
configuration.

### Fix
In `applyEnvOverrides`, read `PORT` as a fallback when `RELAY_SERVER_PORT` is not set. `RELAY_SERVER_PORT` should keep winning when both are present, so existing deployments are unaffected.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `PORT=8080 ./relay-server` listens on 8080
- [ ] `RELAY_SERVER_PORT=3000 PORT=8080 ./relay-server` listens on 3000
- [ ] Neither set → still 3000
- [ ] README config table documents `PORT` as a fallback
title: Support the `PORT` environment variable

body:
### Problem

The README tells users to install `@aossie/thrubox-client`:

```bash
npm install @aossie/thrubox-client
```

That package is not published — `npm view @aossie/thrubox-client` returns a 404.
The published name is `@aossie-org/thrubox-client` (see `package.json`).

Every new user is blocked at the first step of the getting-started guide.

### Fix

Replace `@aossie/thrubox-client` with `@aossie-org/thrubox-client` in README.md.
Three occurrences: the install command, the Quick Start import, and the error
handling example.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All three occurrences updated
- [ ] `npm install @aossie-org/thrubox-client` copied from the README works in a clean directory
title: README install command points at a package that does not exist

### Feature and its Use Cases

Documentation covering how to expose a self-hosted ThruBox-Server instance to the internet after running the Docker container locally.

How would users benefit from it: Users get clear, ready-made guidance for the last step of self-hosting, instead of having to research reverse proxy or tunnel setup on their own.

What scenarios would this feature address: A user runs the Docker container locally (e.g., port 3000 exposed) and wants to make it accessible from the internet using Nginx or Cloudflare Tunnel.

### Additional Context

Scope clarification: we are responsible for providing the Docker container/code that runs locally. Exposing it to the internet is left to the user, guided by our documentation. A fully automatic built-in exposure mechanism is not feasible, since it would require admin access to the user's router, DNS, etc.

title: [FEATURE]: Add documentation for self-hosted deployment (Nginx and Cloudflare Tunnel)
